name: Food allergy and anaphylaxis
definition: A food allergy is when the immune system reacts unusually to specific foods, with reactions that range from mild to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
overview: Food allergy is an immune reaction to a food protein. Symptoms include hives, swelling of the lips, face and eyes, breathing difficulties and tummy problems. A food allergy is different from a food intolerance. The foods children are most often allergic to are cows' milk, hens' eggs, peanuts and tree nuts such as hazelnut and cashew. Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergic reaction that happens very quickly and needs emergency treatment.
causes: Food allergy is an immune reaction to a food protein.
The exact reasons people develop a food allergy are still unclear.
Common triggers include cow's milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, fish and shellfish.
riskFactors: People with a food allergy often have other allergic conditions, such as asthma, hay fever and eczema.
Most children who have a food allergy have had eczema in infancy.
signs: Hives (nettle rash), itching and swelling of the lips, face and eyes.
Breathing difficulties, and in a severe reaction wheezing and swelling of the throat and tongue.
complications: Symptoms that return without contact with the trigger again, known as a biphasic reaction.
diagnosis: The NICE guideline says diagnosis starts with an allergy-focused clinical history and examination. Where the history suggests an IgE-mediated food allergy, skin prick tests or blood tests are offered. For suspected non-IgE-mediated allergy, a trial elimination of the suspected food is used. The NHS lists skin-prick tests, blood tests and sometimes an elimination diet.
treatment: The NHS says antihistamines are used for mild reactions, while adrenaline auto-injectors or a nasal spray are for severe ones. A specialist provides an allergy action plan. Anaphylaxis is treated in hospital straight away, with adrenaline, oxygen and fluids given into a vein.
prevention: The NHS advises avoiding the food that causes the allergy, checking food labels carefully and telling staff at restaurants and cafes about the allergy. NHS guidance for babies says avoiding peanuts and other foods in early childhood can promote rather than prevent allergies.
seekCare: Call 999 for suspected anaphylaxis, such as swelling of the throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, or feeling faint or confused, and tell the operator it is anaphylaxis. The NHS says to use an adrenaline auto-injector straight away if one is available. For other symptoms after eating, the NHS advises speaking to a GP before cutting foods out of the diet.

sections.heading: What is a food allergy?
sections.body:
Allergy UK describes food allergy as the immune system reacting unusually to specific foods. Reactions range from mild to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Food allergy is an immune reaction to a food protein. The exact reasons people develop it are still unclear.

A food allergy is different from a food intolerance. An intolerance usually causes bloating and stomach pain a few hours after eating, rather than an immune reaction. Allergy UK notes that some symptoms resemble food allergy but have other causes, such as lactose intolerance, food poisoning or foods that release histamine.

People with a food allergy often have other allergic conditions, such as asthma, hay fever and eczema. Most children who have a food allergy have had eczema in infancy.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a food allergy?
sections.body:
The NHS lists hives, swelling of the lips, face and eyes, breathing difficulties and tummy problems. Symptoms may start straight after eating the food, or days later. Allergy UK says immediate IgE-mediated reactions occur a few seconds or minutes after eating. Common signs include hives and swelling, and the gut can also be affected, with vomiting and abdominal pain.

Some people have a mix of IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated reactions to the same food. Milder reactions can include feeling hot or cold, anxious or flushed, tingling, itching or burning sensations, or a strange taste in the mouth. A severe reaction is called anaphylaxis, which starts quickly and can cause breathing problems.

sections.heading: Which foods most often cause allergic reactions?
sections.body:
In children, the most common food allergies are to cows' milk, hens' eggs, peanuts and tree nuts such as hazelnut and cashew. Among UK adults, the main triggers include peanuts, tree nuts, crustaceans and plant foods. The NHS lists cow's milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, fish and shellfish as common food triggers of anaphylaxis.

Anaphylaxis UK says milk, egg, soy and wheat allergies are often outgrown. Allergies to peanut, tree nuts, fish and shellfish are often lifelong.

A Food Standards Agency study reported by Anaphylaxis UK estimated that around 6% of UK adults, about 2.4 million people, have a clinically confirmed food allergy. Allergy UK notes that self-reporting tends to overstate how many people have a food allergy.

sections.heading: How is a food allergy diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NICE guideline on food allergy in under 19s says diagnosis starts with an allergy-focused clinical history and examination. When the history suggests an IgE-mediated food allergy, skin prick or blood tests are offered. For suspected non-IgE-mediated allergy, the guideline recommends a trial elimination of the suspected food.

The NICE guideline says that diagnosis should not be made using vega tests, applied kinesiology, hair analysis or serum-specific IgG testing. The NHS describes testing with skin-prick tests, blood tests and sometimes an elimination diet.

NICE advises referral to specialist care for children with an acute systemic reaction, a severe delayed reaction, multiple food allergies, or when the diagnosis is uncertain. The NHS advises speaking to a GP before cutting foods out of the diet.

sections.heading: How is a food allergy treated and managed?
sections.body:
The NHS says antihistamines are used for mild reactions, while adrenaline auto-injectors or a nasal spray are for severe ones. A specialist provides an allergy action plan.

Day-to-day management involves reading food labels and menus carefully and telling the people around the person about the allergy. The NHS says people prescribed them should carry 2 adrenaline auto-injectors or nasal sprays at all times. Anaphylaxis UK helped develop an Adult Allergy Action Plan, and the paediatric allergy action plan has been updated to include young adults.

Allergy UK has called for full ingredient labelling on all food products. NHS guidance for babies says allergenic foods are introduced one at a time from around 6 months.

sections.heading: What is anaphylaxis and what happens in an emergency?
sections.body:
Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergic reaction that happens very quickly. Symptoms usually start within minutes of contact with the trigger. They include swelling of the throat and tongue, fast or difficult breathing, wheezing, feeling faint or confused, and blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue.

The NHS says to call 999 if anaphylaxis is suspected and to tell the operator it is anaphylaxis. It also says to lie down and use an adrenaline auto-injector if one is available. The NHS describes lying the person flat with the legs raised, or sitting them up if breathing is difficult.

Anaphylaxis is treated in hospital straight away, with adrenaline, oxygen and fluids given into a vein. Before leaving hospital, people should be given 2 adrenaline auto-injectors or a prescription for them. An allergy specialist may then carry out tests and give advice. Symptoms can return without contact with the trigger again, which is called a biphasic reaction.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a food allergy and a food intolerance?
faqs.a: A food allergy involves the immune system and can cause hives, swelling, breathing difficulties and tummy problems. A food intolerance usually causes bloating and stomach pain a few hours after eating. The NHS describes the two as different conditions, and testing is used to tell them apart.

faqs.q: Can children grow out of a food allergy?
faqs.a: Anaphylaxis UK says milk, egg, soy and wheat allergies are often outgrown. Allergies to peanut, tree nuts, fish and shellfish are often lifelong. A specialist is the route to advice on whether an individual child has outgrown an allergy.

faqs.q: Can a food allergy cause anaphylaxis?
faqs.a: Yes, food is one of the causes of anaphylaxis, alongside medicines and insect stings. Anaphylaxis is life-threatening and happens very quickly. The NHS says to call 999 and to use an adrenaline auto-injector if one is available.

faqs.q: How common is food allergy in the UK?
faqs.a: A Food Standards Agency study reported by Anaphylaxis UK estimated that around 6% of UK adults have a clinically confirmed food allergy. That is about 2.4 million people. More adults report reactions to food than have a confirmed allergy.

faqs.q: Should foods be cut out of the diet if an allergy is suspected?
faqs.a: The NHS advises speaking to a GP before cutting foods out of the diet. For babies, NHS guidance says avoiding peanuts and other foods in early childhood can promote rather than prevent allergies. The NICE guideline describes a trial elimination of a suspected food as part of diagnosing some types of allergy.
